label: Prostaglandin pathway
explanation: The schematic traces membrane phospholipids through phospholipase A2 to arachidonic acid and, via COX-1/COX-2, to PGH2 and tissue-specific prostaglandins. Thromboxane A2, generated by platelets, drives platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction; prostacyclin (PGI2) opposes it with vasodilation and inhibition of aggregation.

label: NAPQI pathway
explanation: A minor fraction of acetaminophen is oxidized by cytochrome P450 to NAPQI, normally detoxified by glutathione conjugation. When glucuronidation and sulfation are saturated and glutathione is depleted, NAPQI accumulates and binds covalently to hepatic proteins, causing oxidative and mitochondrial injury and centrilobular necrosis. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione.

label: Rumack-Matthew nomogram
explanation: The Rumack-Matthew nomogram is validated only for single acute ingestions and is applied from 4 hours post-ingestion, once absorption and distribution are largely complete; levels drawn earlier can underestimate the peak. A concentration falling above the treatment line indicates a need for N-acetylcysteine.

label: Adrenergic receptors
explanation: The beta-adrenergic receptors (beta1, beta2, beta3) are Gs-coupled GPCRs; activation stimulates adenylyl cyclase and raises intracellular cAMP, whereas alpha1 uses Gq (IP3/DAG) and alpha2 uses Gi (lowers cAMP).

label: Cholinergic receptors
explanation: Nicotinic receptors (nM in muscle, nN in neurons) are ionotropic ligand-gated cation channels activated by ACh, while all muscarinic subtypes (M1-M5) are metabotropic GPCRs coupling to Gq or Gi.

label: Adrenergic receptors
explanation: Beta1 receptors are Gs-coupled; cardiac beta1 activation raises cAMP, increasing sinoatrial rate (positive chronotropy) and myocardial contractility (positive inotropy).

label: Cushing syndrome
explanation: Chronic glucocorticoid exposure suppresses fibroblast activity and collagen synthesis while promoting protein breakdown, thinning the dermis. The weakened, thin skin stretches over expanding central fat and tears, exposing dermal vasculature as the characteristic wide purple striae seen in iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.

label: Adrenergic receptors
explanation: The tree depicts adrenergic receptors (alpha1, alpha2, beta1-3), which are the receptors for the catecholamines norepinephrine and epinephrine.

label: Adrenergic G-proteins
explanation: Beta-adrenergic receptors are Gs-coupled; their activation stimulates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP to produce effects such as increased cardiac contractility and rate.

label: Lipoprotein metabolism
explanation: The diagram traces cholesterol and triglyceride handling across hepatic synthesis, VLDL/LDL/HDL trafficking in blood, and intestinal absorption/reabsorption of cholesterol and bile acids, i.e., integrated lipoprotein metabolism, the pathway statins act on.

label: Prostate
explanation: The right panel shows relaxation of prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle with a dilated urethra, the effect of a selective alpha-1 (alpha-1A) receptor antagonist. Tamsulosin is the uroselective alpha-1A blocker used to relieve the obstructive urinary symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia. Finasteride shrinks the gland by a different (5-alpha-reductase) mechanism, sildenafil is a PDE-5 inhibitor, phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist that would worsen obstruction, and propranolol is a beta-blocker.

label: Adrenergic receptors
explanation: The tree depicts the adrenergic (catecholaminergic) receptor family, split into alpha (alpha1, alpha2) and beta (beta1, beta2, beta3) subtypes. All of these receptors are activated by the endogenous catecholamines norepinephrine and epinephrine, which is why they are the targets of adrenergic agonists (sympathomimetics).

label: Cholinergic receptors
explanation: Unlike the muscarinic subtypes, which are G-protein-coupled receptors (hence the Gq/Gi tags in the figure), nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels that open directly on acetylcholine binding, allowing rapid cation influx and depolarization. The absence of a G-protein label on the nicotinic branch reflects this ionotropic mechanism.

label: Adrenergic receptors
explanation: The alpha1 subtype couples to Gq, activating phospholipase C, generating IP3/DAG and raising intracellular calcium, which drives vascular smooth-muscle contraction and vasoconstriction. Bronchodilation and increased contractility are beta effects, and presynaptic inhibition of norepinephrine release is an alpha2 effect.

label: Acid secretion
brick: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Blockers
explanation: The parietal cell is the effector cell of gastric acid secretion; it houses the H+/K+-ATPase and responds to acetylcholine (M3), gastrin, and histamine (H2). G cells secrete gastrin, ECL cells release histamine, chief cells secrete pepsinogen, and D cells release somatostatin.

label: Parietal cell
brick: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Blockers
explanation: H2 receptor antagonists reversibly block histamine at the H2 receptor, reducing the cAMP-dependent pathway that activates the proton pump. This is less complete than PPIs, which irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase itself, the final common pathway.

label: PPI adverse effects
brick: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Blockers
explanation: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase, raising gastric pH. The persistently low acidity impairs absorption of Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe2+ and vitamin B12 and removes the acid barrier to enteric pathogens, driving increased risk of malabsorption, osteoporosis, C. difficile infection, and pneumonia.

label: Drug routes
explanation: Parenteral routes (e.g., intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous) deliver drug outside of and bypassing the gastrointestinal tract, entering the systemic circulation directly through vascular access, in contrast to enteral routes that use the GI tract.

label: First-pass metabolism
explanation: Orally absorbed drug travels via the portal vein to the liver, where hepatic (and gut wall) enzymes metabolize a portion before it enters the systemic circulation. This first-pass metabolism lowers oral bioavailability compared with routes that bypass the portal circulation.

label: Adrenergic receptors
explanation: Every adrenergic receptor shown in this classification tree (the alpha-1, alpha-2, and beta-1/2/3 subtypes) is a G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR). These seven-transmembrane receptors act through heterotrimeric G proteins to drive downstream second-messenger signaling rather than opening ion channels directly or possessing intrinsic kinase activity.

label: Corpora cavernosa
explanation: Erection results from nitric oxide-driven relaxation of the arterial and trabecular smooth muscle within the corpora cavernosa, which increases arterial inflow and fills the sinusoidal spaces with blood, producing rigidity. This is the target pathway of PDE-5 inhibitors.

label: Excitation-contraction coupling
explanation: The diagram depicts excitation-contraction coupling: depolarization opens L-type Ca2+ channels, and the resulting Ca2+ entry triggers further Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (calcium-induced calcium release), which drives contraction. Blocking these channels reduces this trigger, not the upstream nerve signaling or Na+/K+ ionic currents.

label: Calcium channel blocker
explanation: Blocking the L-type Ca2+ channel lowers intracellular calcium in vascular smooth muscle, reducing myosin light-chain phosphorylation and causing relaxation and vasodilation. The other options are the opposite of, or unrelated to, reduced calcium influx.

label: Cholinergic synapse
explanation: Anticholinergics are muscarinic antagonists that act by competitive inhibition, binding the receptor without activating it so that endogenous acetylcholine cannot exert its effect on the target cell.

label: Anticholinergic toxidrome
explanation: The illustration depicts the anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) toxidrome. Physostigmine, a centrally acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, raises synaptic acetylcholine to overcome muscarinic blockade and is the antidote. Atropine would worsen it, pralidoxime treats organophosphate poisoning, naloxone reverses opioids, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

label: H1 receptor
explanation: The diagram depicts the H1 histamine receptor, a seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptor. Histamine released from the activated mast cell binds this GPCR to trigger downstream effects (itching, swelling, inflammation); an H1 antagonist occupies the receptor and leaves it inactive, preventing signaling. H1 receptors are not ion channels, kinase receptors, or nuclear receptors.

label: Organophosphate
explanation: Organophosphorus inhibitors are tetrahedral, mimicking the transition state formed during carboxyl ester hydrolysis at the enzyme's active site, which allows them to bind acetylcholinesterase and phosphorylate it.

label: Opioid receptors
explanation: Most clinically used opioid agonists act primarily at mu (μ) receptors, which mediate analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression, and dependence. Kappa and delta receptors modulate these effects and contribute to other actions but are not the main analgesic target.

label: CNS opioid receptors
explanation: In the dorsal horn, presynaptic opioid receptors reduce calcium influx and inhibit release of excitatory neurotransmitters (e.g., substance P, glutamate) from primary afferents, while postsynaptic hyperpolarization decreases transmission of nociceptive signals, producing analgesia.

label: RAAS pathway
explanation: The diagram shows renin acting on angiotensinogen to form angiotensin I, ACE converting it to angiotensin II, and downstream aldosterone secretion, which is the classic renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) that regulates blood pressure and volume.

label: Glomerular filtration
explanation: Angiotensin II normally constricts the efferent arteriole to maintain glomerular pressure and filtration. When RAAS inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR fall, which can precipitate prerenal acute kidney injury in low-flow states.

label: NSAID effect
explanation: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, constricting the afferent arteriole and reducing renal blood flow. Combined with RAAS inhibitors that dilate the efferent arteriole, this greatly increases the risk of acute kidney injury.

label: Metformin
brick: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors
explanation: The agent depicted is metformin. In skeletal muscle it activates AMPK, the cellular sensor of AMP:ATP and ADP:ATP ratios, which drives GLUT-4 translocation to the membrane and increases insulin-mediated glucose uptake. Metformin also decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis and reduces intestinal glucose absorption, together improving insulin sensitivity.

label: Lipid bilayer
explanation: The neutral, uncharged (unionized) form of a drug is lipophilic and diffuses freely through the fatty acyl core of the lipid bilayer, whereas the charged (ionized) form is hydrophilic and is repelled, as shown by the blocked pathway. Passive crossing is therefore governed primarily by the drug's ionization state.

label: NSAID COX selectivity
explanation: Highly COX-2 selective agents reduce endothelial prostacyclin (PGI2) while leaving platelet-derived thromboxane A2 relatively intact, shifting the balance toward platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction. This underlies the increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke that led to withdrawal of several coxibs.

label: Antagonist
explanation: An antagonist occupies the receptor and prevents agonist binding/activation, producing no downstream effect, in contrast to the agonist which activates signaling.

label: Graded dose-response
brick: Pharmacodynamics: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index
explanation: A graded dose-response curve plots the continuous magnitude of drug effect against drug concentration for a single patient, rising sigmoidally to a maximum (Emax) with the half-maximal effect defining the EC50.

label: Quantal dose curve
brick: Pharmacodynamics: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index
explanation: A quantal dose-effect frequency curve is a normal (Gaussian) distribution; the dose at its center, where 50% of the population shows the defined all-or-none response, is the median effective dose, ED50.

label: Therapeutic index
brick: Pharmacodynamics: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index
explanation: The greater the separation between the efficacy and toxicity curves, the larger the therapeutic index and the safer the drug, because effective and toxic doses overlap less.

label: Dose-response curves
brick: Pharmacodynamics: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index
explanation: The therapeutic index is the ratio of a dose producing toxicity/lethality to a dose producing the desired effect (e.g., LD50/ED50 or TD50/ED50); a larger ratio indicates a safer drug.

label: Arachidonic acid pathway
explanation: The rightmost branch product is Thromboxane A2 (TxA2), synthesized largely by platelets. TxA2 is a potent promoter of platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, which is why aspirin's inhibition of its synthesis produces an antithrombotic effect.

label: Aspirin acetylation
explanation: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates a serine in the active site of COX-1, fully inactivating it. For COX-2, the same acetylation does not stop the enzyme but converts its cyclooxygenase activity into a lipoxygenase (LOX) activity, generating anti-inflammatory lipoxins rather than prostaglandins.

label: Zero-order kinetics
brick: Pharmacokinetics: Volume of Distribution and Elimination Kinetics
explanation: A constant absolute amount of drug removed per unit time, independent of concentration, yields a straight line on a linear plot, characteristic of zero-order kinetics.

label: Zero-order elimination
brick: Pharmacokinetics: Volume of Distribution and Elimination Kinetics
explanation: Ethanol (along with phenytoin and aspirin at high doses) is eliminated at a constant amount per unit time because its metabolic pathway is saturated, defining zero-order kinetics.

label: First-order kinetics
brick: Pharmacokinetics: Volume of Distribution and Elimination Kinetics
explanation: First-order kinetics removes a constant proportion of drug per unit time, so the elimination rate is proportional to concentration and the curve decays exponentially on a linear scale.

label: First-order elimination
brick: Pharmacokinetics: Volume of Distribution and Elimination Kinetics
explanation: Because a constant proportion is removed per unit time, the time for concentration to fall by half is fixed regardless of the starting concentration, so half-life is constant in first-order kinetics.

label: Steady state
brick: Pharmacokinetics: Volume of Distribution and Elimination Kinetics
explanation: A continuous IV infusion inputs drug at a constant rate equal to the elimination rate at steady state, so concentration plateaus without the peak-trough swings seen with intermittent oral dosing.
